title: Who holds the brake?
brief: An agent is about to act. Decide whether a person approves first, is pulled in on a trigger, reviews a sample afterwards or only sees a log, while reversibility, reach, volume and regulatory class are still open.

blocks.md:
Oversight is a brake with a price. **Approve before action** stops harm before it lands but adds friction and invites rubber-stamping. **Escalate on a trigger** pulls a person in only for hard cases. **Sampled review with undo** accepts that some mistakes land and relies on cheap reversal. **Log and alert only** gives accountability after the fact, not a brake.

Law and design heuristics agree on the shape. For high-risk systems Article 14 expects oversight proportionate to risk, autonomy and context: people can understand the system's limits, stay aware of automation bias, interpret output, decide not to use or override it, and interrupt it with a stop control. For biometric identification under Annex III point 1(a), two competent people must verify separately before action [[r5]]. Meta's Rule of Two says that when a session needs untrusted input, sensitive access and the ability to change state or communicate externally, require human approval [[r23]]. A reviewer who sees a tool name and a yes button is not exercising oversight, so design the screen to show the evidence and the arguments.

blocks.title: Oversight patterns
blocks.intro: Each pattern names where it wins, where it loses and what flips the choice.

options.name: Approve before action
options.summary: A person approves each action, or each action above a threshold, before it runs. A two-person variant adds a second independent reviewer.
pros: A named approver gives clear accountability
options.bestWhen: Irreversible or externally visible actions at modest volume.
options.avoidWhen: Thousands of reversible actions a day.

options.name: Escalate on a trigger
options.summary: The agent acts alone until a rule fires: low confidence, a large amount, sensitive data or a policy hit.
pros: Humans see only the hard cases
cons: Only as good as the trigger
A narrow trigger hides costly misses
options.bestWhen: High volume with a risky tail you can describe.
options.avoidWhen: Irreversible actions where one missed trigger is unacceptable.

options.name: Sampled review with undo
options.summary: Actions run, a sample is reviewed afterwards and mistakes are reversed.
options.bestWhen: High volume, reversible actions with low reach.

options.name: Log and alert only
options.summary: Record every action and alert on anomalies, with no person in the path.
cons: Gives no means to intervene, which Article 14 expects for high-risk systems
options.avoidWhen: Anything with external reach or a regulated use.

blocks.title: How much human oversight does this action need?
blocks.prompt: Set how reversible the action is, how far it reaches, how many a day and whether the use is high-risk under the AI Act. The best brake changes.

values.label: High-risk use under the AI Act

options.name: Escalate on a trigger
options.summary: A person joins when a rule fires.

options.name: Sampled review with undo
options.summary: Review a sample after the fact.

easy.why: Friction for an action you can undo.

irrev.why: A human gate before the point of no return.

high.why: The queue grows and approvals become rubber stamps.
Article 14 expects the means to override and stop.

costly.why: Reserve it for the costliest cases.

irrev.why: Two independent checks before the point of no return.

many.why: Many affected people justify two reviewers.

high.why: Some high-risk uses require two separate verifications (Article 14(5)).

easy.why: Pull a person in only when unsure.

irrev.why: A confidence trigger alone is not a gate for irreversible actions.

many.why: A missed trigger is visible to many.

high.why: Humans see only the hard cases.
Needs documented triggers and a real override path.

irrev.why: Review arrives after the point of no return.

many.why: A bad batch spreads before anyone samples.

high.why: The only way to cover thousands of actions.
Not sufficient alone for high-risk oversight.

costly.why: A log does not undo harm.

high.why: Logs are required but are not oversight.

blocks.takeaway: Reversibility and reach pick the family: approval for irreversible, sampling for reversible. Volume and regulatory class then adjust it. Say which dial moved you.

items.symptom: Approval rate sits near 100% and decisions take two seconds.
items.cause: Volume or a bare yes or no screen has turned approval into rubber-stamping, the automation bias Article 14 warns about.
items.fix: Show arguments and evidence, seed known-bad items and track the catch rate, and move low-risk actions to sampled review.

items.symptom: A risky tool runs after a client message claims it was approved.
items.cause: An unbound or replayed approval. By default the framework authorizes a call only when the response matches a pending request in the same session.
items.fix: Keep approval binding on. If you disable it, bind approvals to request id, user and session in your own gate [[r16]].

items.symptom: The gated tool is never called, yet the same effect happens.
items.cause: The gate sits on one tool while a second tool, an MCP server or an API reaches the same effect.
items.fix: Gate by action class at a gateway or policy layer and test every path that can produce the effect.

items.symptom: Escalations are rare and a costly mistake slips through.
items.cause: A confidence trigger that is too narrow or poorly calibrated.
items.fix: Add risk triggers (amount, external recipient, data class), audit what was not escalated and tune with seeded cases.

blocks.title: Gate a tool and read the approval request
blocks.caption: Reply with req.to_function_approval_response(True or False) in a new run on the same session.

blocks.title: Wrap the function so it needs approval

quiz.q: An agent issues refunds. Refunds under 20 units are easy to reverse and run in the thousands each day. Refunds above 5,000 units are hard to claw back and run a few times a day. Which oversight design fits?
options: Sampled review with undo for small refunds and approval for large ones
Log and alert only for every refund
quiz.explain: Reversibility and volume point in opposite directions across the two tiers, so you tier the brake. Approving thousands of small refunds creates a queue and rubber-stamping, logging alone gives no brake before a 5,000 unit loss, and two-person review for everything is unaffordable at volume.

quiz.q: What does this setting risk unless your application enforces an equivalent binding?
options: Tool calls stop being gated at all
Approvals are shared across users in the same tenant
A fabricated or replayed response can authorize a privileged tool call
quiz.explain: By default a local approval authorizes a call only when it matches a pending request in the same session. Disabling the binding restores unbound behaviour, so a forged or replayed response can approve a privileged call. Gating itself stays on, there is no one-minute expiry in that setting and it does not share approvals across tenants.

quiz.q: Select every control that reduces automation bias on an approval screen (design reasoning, consistent with Article 14).
options: Show the arguments, retrieved evidence and a diff of the change
Require a written reason for approvals above a threshold
Seed known-bad items and track the reviewer catch rate
Preselect the approve button to save time
Track decision time and approval rate per reviewer
quiz.explain: Evidence, justification, seeded errors and decision metrics all make careless approval visible or harder. A preselected approve button does the opposite and encourages the automation bias Article 14 asks overseers to resist.

takeaways: Reversibility and reach choose the family of brake. Volume and regulatory class adjust it.
Approval without evidence is not oversight. Show arguments, seed bad items and measure the catch rate.
Bind approvals to the pending request, the user and the session so they cannot be replayed.
Gate by action class, not by one tool, or the effect leaks through another path.
When all three Rule of Two properties are needed, a human approves.
